title: Pruning: cutting back to grow stronger
description: It feels like vandalism — taking shears to a healthy plant and removing good growth. Gardeners prune anyway, because a plant with less to feed often grows more of what matters. The rule works on calendars, too.

body.heading: Why less plant can mean more growth
paragraphs: Pruning is the deliberate removal of parts of a plant — dead, damaged, crossing or simply excess growth. Dead and diseased wood goes first, because it invites trouble. Crossing branches go next, because they rub wounds into each other. Then comes the shaping cut: removing growth that shades the centre or crowds the strongest shoots.

The plant's response is the surprise. Roots that were feeding twenty shoots now feed twelve, so the twelve get more water, more minerals and more light, and they grow longer, flower better and fruit heavier. The plant was never short of effort — it was short of focus.

body.heading: Prune one thing of yours
paragraphs: Commitments grow like shrubs: vigorously, in every direction, until the centre is dark. A monthly prune asks the gardener's three questions of your calendar. What is dead or diseased — kept alive only by guilt? What is crossing — two good things rubbing each other raw by competing for the same hour? What is crowding the strongest growth?

Cut kindly and cut cleanly: resign properly, hand over notes, thank people. Then watch what gardeners watch — the remaining shoots, lengthening. Growth is not always adding. Sometimes growth is the brave arithmetic of subtraction.

takeaway: Pruning removes dead, crossing and crowding growth so a plant's roots can feed fewer shoots better — the same subtraction that helps an overgrown calendar.
